entry.title: Should you disable admin-cli and account in a production Keycloak realm?
entry.summary: Disabling Keycloak's built-in clients is mostly the wrong lever. Turn off Direct Access Grants everywhere, remove what each client actually exposes, and put a CAPTCHA in front of the flows bots hit. Measured on Keycloak 26.8.1.
entry.content:
Mostly no, and the question points at the wrong lever. Every Keycloak realm ships with the same six client IDs, so the first thing an automated attacker does after finding /realms/<name>/.well-known/openid-configuration is post grant_type=password&client_id=admin-cli to the token endpoint and read the error. The probe costs nothing, it arrives from a different IP every time, and with LLM-driven tooling the follow-up is a dictionary run that adapts to whatever your realm answers. The exposure is not that admin-cli exists. It is that admin-cli is a public client with Direct Access Grants on and full scope on, and any other client configured that way is exactly as dangerous. Turning the password grant off everywhere is mandatory. Disabling clients is a secondary, case-by-case call, and for account it is usually the wrong one.

Everything below was reproduced against Keycloak 26.8.1, and every error string is copied out of a real response.

What the probe sees​

One request, POST /realms/prod/protocol/openid-connect/token with grant_type=password, client_id=admin-cli and a wrong password, against four states of the same realm:

Realm stateResponseWhat the attacker learns
Defaults400 {"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"Invalid user credentials"}Password grant is live. Start the dictionary.
Direct Access Grants off on admin-cli400 {"error":"unauthorized_client","error_description":"Client not allowed for direct access grants"}Client exists, door shut. Try the other five IDs.
admin-cli disabled401 {"error":"invalid_client","error_description":"Invalid client or Invalid client credentials"}Same answer as a client that never existed.
Client policy rejecting the grant400 {"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"resource owner password credentials grant is prohibited."}No client here takes a password. Move on.

A wrong password and an unknown username return the same body, so usernames do not leak. Which clients exist, and which accept passwords, does.

admin-cli: the grant is the problem, not the client​

Out of the box, admin-cli is the only built-in client with the password grant on:

ClientPublicDirect Access GrantsFull scope allowed
admin-cliyesonon
security-admin-consoleyesoffon
account, account-consoleyesoffoff
realm-management, brokerbearer-onlyoffoff

It bypasses your browser flow. The default direct grant flow is username, password, then a conditional OTP step that only fires for users with a TOTP device. Side by side with the browser flow on the same server:

direct grant                       browser (forms subflow)
  Username Validation  REQUIRED      Username Password Form     REQUIRED
  Password             REQUIRED      Browser - Conditional 2FA  CONDITIONAL
  Conditional OTP      CONDITIONAL     Condition - credential   REQUIRED
    OTP                REQUIRED        OTP Form                 ALTERNATIVE
                                       WebAuthn Authenticator   DISABLED
                                       Recovery Codes           DISABLED

No WebAuthn, no passkeys, no CAPTCHA, none of the steps you added to the browser flow. A passkey-only user gets a token for a password alone. RFC 9700, the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, says the password grant "MUST NOT be used" and "is not designed to work with two-factor authentication".

It is the cleaner target for credential stuffing. Brute force detection does cover the token endpoint, but it is per user. A spray of one guess per username per window, from a rotating pool of residential IPs, slides under per-user lockout and under per-IP limits at the proxy at the same time. Edge rate limiting is worth having; it is not what stops this.

Disabling it does not shrink the Admin API. Admin requests are authorized from the roles of the user behind the token, filtered by what the client may scope. A realm admin's admin-cli token carries no roles at all (it is a lightweight token) and still gets 200 from /admin/realms/prod/users. The same user through an application client with Full scope allowed on gets the same 200, now with every realm-management role visible in resource_access. With Full scope allowed off on that client, the call returns 403, and 26.8.1 logs a warning for every token issued with the switch on:

WARN  [org.keycloak.protocol.oidc.endpoints.TokenEndpoint.full-scope-allowed] Client 'webapp' in the realm
'prod' has 'Full scope allowed' switch enabled. This client switch is deprecated and will be removed in the
future. Please update your client settings to disable the switch and configure needed roles, which this
client application needs, to the client role scope

So the hardening is per realm:

  • Reject the password grant with a client policy. A client profile with the reject-ropc-grant executor, Auto-configure on, bound to a policy with the any-client condition. Every client then answers resource owner password credentials grant is prohibited., and any client created or updated afterwards has Direct Access Grants switched off for you. Set Auto-configure explicitly: left unset, client creation fails with a null pointer on 26.8.1. The same executor ships inside the built-in oauth-2-1-for-public-client and oauth-2-1-for-confidential-client profiles.
  • Automation uses service accounts. A confidential client, client_credentials only, with the specific realm-management roles it needs. A provisioner client holding only manage-users lists users with 200 and is refused on /clients with 403, which is the shape a user-sync job should have. realm-admin belongs to people behind MFA, not to a secret in a pipeline.
  • Full scope allowed off on every application client, enforced with the full-scope-disabled executor if you have many.
  • Non-master realms: disable admin-cli once nothing runs kcadm against them. In master, keep it only while tooling depends on it and restrict /admin/* and /realms/master/* at the edge. On a Phase Two cluster, admin-path IP restrictions do this and master is not exposed to customers.

account and account-console: remove the roles, not the client​

account is not a login surface. It is the audience and role container for the Account REST API: /realms/prod/account/ accepts a token that carries manage-account or view-profile under resource_access.account, and users get those roles through default-roles-<realm>.

Disabling it does work as a kill switch; console and API both return 404 {"error":"account management not enabled"}. It also has a side effect that changed in Keycloak 26. execute-actions-email and send-verify-email called without a client_id used to fail with 400 Client is not enabled. Since 26.0.0 Keycloak creates a confidential client named _system on the fly and issues the email link against it:

WARN  [org.keycloak.models.utils.SystemClientUtil] Client 'account' not available. Creating system client
'_system' for system operations

The reset email still arrives, and the next audit finds a client nobody created. If the goal is no self-service through Keycloak:

  • Disable account-console, the PKCE public client behind the UI, or bind a Deny-access flow override to it as Account Console describes.
  • Remove manage-account and manage-account-links from default-roles-<realm>. Measured: reads of /account/ still return 200 through view-profile, writes return 403. Remove view-profile too and the token loses the account audience entirely, so every call returns 401.

If you keep self-service, the residual risk is a hijacked session changing credentials. Require re-authentication for credential changes with kc_action and max_age, keep SSO idle short, and require the current password on password change.

security-admin-console, realm-management, broker​

security-admin-console is a bigger surface than either client above: in a non-master realm it is the realm-scoped admin UI at /admin/<realm>/console/, public, PKCE, Full scope allowed on. If no realm-scoped administrator uses it, disable it; the login redirect then renders Keycloak's Client disabled. page. Otherwise keep it and block the path at the edge.

realm-management and broker are bearer-only role containers. There is no flow to attack, and the admin roles and the broker read-token role hang off them. Leave them alone.

Rate limiting is not enough: put a CAPTCHA in the flow​

Per-IP limits assume the attacker has an IP. Per-user lockout assumes they want one user. Credential stuffing today has neither property, which is why a CAPTCHA earns its place: it taxes the automation, not the address. Keycloak's built-in reCAPTCHA only covers registration, so for login you need an extension. The Cloudflare Turnstile integration in our open-source keycloak-magic-link extension is the one we recommend and ship on every Phase Two cluster. It is three authenticators sharing one configuration (site key, secret, action), which is what makes it a flow edit rather than a project:

  • Cloudflare Turnstile Username Password Form replaces the stock login form with the widget embedded in the page. Unconfigured, it behaves exactly like the original. Its Verify email on CAPTCHA failure option turns a failed challenge into a forced email verification instead of a hard block, so a real user on a flaky network still gets in and a bot does not.
  • Condition - Turnstile Failed gates a 2FA subflow on the CAPTCHA result: Required means only sessions that failed the challenge are asked for a second factor, Disabled means 2FA for everyone with a factor enrolled. Adaptive friction from one requirement toggle.
  • Cloudflare Turnstile validation is a standalone challenge page to place before any step that sends email, such as magic link or email OTP, so bots cannot turn your SMTP relay into a flood.
  • The registration form action validates the challenge on sign-up and skips it for users who are already identified, so invitations keep working while bulk account creation, and the abusive takeovers that follow it, stop.

Setup is two settings: https://challenges.cloudflare.com in frame-src under Security Defenses, and the cloudflare-turnstile login theme on the realm or one client. No image puzzles, which matters when the people solving it are your customers.

This closes the loop with the first section. A CAPTCHA protects flows that render a page. The token endpoint renders nothing, so with the password grant enabled an attacker simply takes the path without one. The two controls only work together.

The checklist​

ClientDefaultProduction
admin-clipublic, password grant on, full scope onPassword grant off, policy-enforced. Disable in non-master realms once nothing uses it.
security-admin-consolepublic, PKCE, full scope onDisable where no realm-scoped admins exist, or block /admin/* at the edge.
accountpublic, role container, API audienceKeep enabled. Remove manage-account and manage-account-links from default roles if self-service is unwanted.
account-consolepublic, PKCEDisable or deny-flow when self-service is unwanted.
realm-management, brokerbearer-onlyLeave alone.
Your application clientswhatever you clickedPassword grant off, full scope off, PKCE, Turnstile on login and registration.

All of this fits in a realm export you keep in version control. If you would rather start from a realm configured this way, Phase Two runs managed Keycloak with Turnstile, magic links and admin-path restrictions included, and a 30-day Starter trial from $149/month. Self-hosting is the right call for plenty of teams: the production readiness checklist covers the server-side settings next to these, brute force detection covers the per-user side, and the WAF question covers what belongs at the edge. The go-live checklist is where it all lands before launch.

entry.title: Keycloak 502 Bad Gateway behind a reverse proxy
entry.summary: A Keycloak 502 Bad Gateway is always the proxy, never Keycloak. Six error-log lines, what each one means, and the fix — measured on Keycloak 26.8.1 and nginx 1.29.
entry.content:
A Keycloak 502 Bad Gateway never comes from Keycloak. RFC 9110 defines 502 as a status a gateway emits about its upstream — so the proxy is telling you it could not get a usable response out of Keycloak, and the explanation is in the proxy's error log rather than anywhere in Keycloak's configuration. Start there, every time. In nginx there are only six lines that produce a 502 in front of Keycloak, each maps to one cause, and three of the six are the Quarkus-era port layout catching out a config written for an older release.

Everything below was reproduced against Keycloak 26.8.1 behind nginx 1.29, and every error string is copied out of a real run.

The six lines, and what each one means​

Run one failing request and read error.log. This table is the whole diagnosis:

nginx error.logWhat it meansFix
connect() failed (111: Connection refused)Nothing is listening on the port you proxy toCheck the port matrix below
no live upstreams while connecting to upstreamThe proxy has marked every backend down — usually a health check on the wrong portProbe :9000/health/ready, not :8080/health
SSL_do_handshake() failed (SSL: error:0A00010B:SSL routines::wrong version number)proxy_pass https:// to a plaintext KeycloakUse http://, or give Keycloak a certificate
upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response headerproxy_pass http:// to a TLS KeycloakUse https://, or set http-enabled=true
upstream SSL certificate verify error: (18:self-signed certificate)Re-encrypt mode, and Keycloak's certificate is not in the proxy's trust storeTrust it explicitly, or terminate at the edge
upstream sent too big header while reading response headerA response header exceeded proxy_buffer_sizeRaise the buffers — see below

If the log says upstream timed out, you have a 504, not a 502, and it is a different problem. Keycloak answered too slowly; the proxy never failed to reach it.

The port matrix​

Most Connection refused reports are this table. Which ports Keycloak opens depends on the start command and on whether you gave it key material — and nothing about the proxy config tells you which case you are in:

Keycloak started with:8080:8443
start-devlistensrefused
start, certificate configuredrefusedlistens
start --http-enabled=true, no certificatelistensrefused
start, no certificate, no http-enabledthe server does not start—

That last row is the one that wastes an afternoon. The container exits before it binds anything, the proxy reports Connection refused, and the actual message is in the Keycloak log:

Key material not provided to setup HTTPS. Please configure your keys/certificates,
or if HTTPS access is not needed see the `http-enabled` option. If you meant to
start the server in development mode, see the `start-dev` command.

The second row is the other half. A config that worked against start-dev on a laptop and proxies to http://keycloak:8080 finds nothing there once the server has a certificate, because production Keycloak does not open 8080 unless you ask it to.

Note also that :9000 is a third listener, for health and metrics, and it only opens when you enable one of them. Keycloak's own guidance is that you should not proxy it: "You should not proxy port 9000 because health checks and metrics use that port directly, and you do not want to expose this information to external callers."

The TLS mismatch, in both directions​

The two handshake errors are the same mistake pointing opposite ways, and they are worth telling apart because the second one does not look like a TLS problem at all.

# proxy_pass https://keycloak:8080  — proxy speaks TLS, Keycloak speaks plaintext
SSL_do_handshake() failed (SSL: error:0A00010B:SSL routines::wrong version number)
  while SSL handshaking to upstream

# proxy_pass http://keycloak:8443  — proxy speaks plaintext, Keycloak speaks TLS
upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream

upstream prematurely closed connection is a generic string that also appears when a backend crashes mid-request, which is why it sends people hunting for an OOM kill that never happened. Before you go looking at memory, check the scheme against the port.

If you run re-encrypt — the mode the Keycloak docs recommend for production, where the proxy terminates the client connection and opens a new TLS connection to Keycloak — then verification is the next thing to get wrong:

upstream SSL certificate verify error: (18:self-signed certificate)
  while SSL handshaking to upstream

nginx does not verify upstream certificates by default, so this only appears once you have correctly turned proxy_ssl_verify on. Point proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate at the CA that signed Keycloak's certificate rather than at the system bundle, and keep proxy_ssl_server_name on so SNI matches.

When only the login page 502s​

This is the one that reads as impossible: the discovery document is fine, the admin console is fine, and /protocol/openid-connect/auth returns 502 for some clients and not others.

Keycloak sets KC_RESTART on the authorization endpoint — an encrypted token carrying the auth session, including the redirect_uri and the state your application sent. So the size of the response headers is controlled by your client, not by Keycloak. Measuring the response header block against the length of state, with a short redirect_uri:

state lengthKeycloak response headersThrough nginx defaults
01,728 B200
8003,148 B200
1,3204,076 B200
1,3404,111 B502
1,5004,396 B502

The break is at 4,096 bytes, which is nginx's default proxy_buffer_size — one memory page. Roughly 1.8 bytes of response header per byte of state, so an OIDC library that packs a PKCE verifier, a nonce and a return URL into state, or a client with a long redirect_uri, crosses it while a simpler client on the same realm never does. Raising the buffers clears it:

location / {
    proxy_pass http://keycloak:8080;
    proxy_buffer_size        16k;
    proxy_buffers          8 16k;
    proxy_busy_buffers_size  32k;
}

Re-measured with those three lines, a state of 3,000 characters and 7,061 bytes of response headers returns 200. This is a header-size limit, not a token-size limit — the request-side version of the same squeeze shows up as HTTP 431 and is a different fix.

When every request 502s after an upgrade​

Keycloak serves health and metrics on the management port, and /health on the main port is simply not a route:

:8080:9000
/health404200
/health/ready404200

A readiness probe or load-balancer health check still pointed at http://keycloak:8080/health gets a 404, marks the backend unhealthy, and every request through the proxy becomes a 502 even though Keycloak is serving traffic normally. The log line is the giveaway, because it is about the pool rather than about one connection:

no live upstreams while connecting to upstream

Two things to check together: the probe URL must be :9000/health/ready, and health-enabled must be true — the management port does not open at all unless health or metrics is enabled, so a probe against :9000 on a default server is also refused.

What a 502 is not​

Three failures sit next to this one and none of them produce a 502:

  • 403 Forbidden on requests through the proxy means proxy-headers is unset. The Keycloak docs are explicit: "If you are using a reverse proxy for anything other than TLS passthrough and do not set the proxy-headers option, then by default you will see 403 Forbidden responses to requests via the proxy that perform origin checking." Set proxy-headers=xforwarded (or forwarded), and never with TLS passthrough.
  • 504 Gateway Timeout is Keycloak being slow, not unreachable.
  • A login that bounces is a cookie problem, covered in Keycloak infinite redirect loop at login.

Stop it recurring​

Pin the proxy-side settings next to the server-side ones, so the pair cannot drift apart:

conf/keycloak.conf
hostname=https://auth.example.com
http-enabled=true
proxy-headers=xforwarded
proxy-trusted-addresses=10.0.0.0/8
health-enabled=true

Then assert it in CI. One request through the public URL for /realms/<realm>/.well-known/openid-configuration and one for :9000/health/ready catches every cause above on the commit that introduces it — the first fails on a wrong port, a wrong scheme, an untrusted certificate or undersized buffers, and the second fails on the probe that would otherwise take the whole pool down an hour later. The Keycloak production checklist has the rest of the settings that belong in that file.

A 502 is a short debugging session once you accept that the answer is in the proxy's log and not in Keycloak's. If you would rather not own the proxy, the certificate chain and the port layout across upgrades, Phase Two runs managed Keycloak with a 30-day Starter trial from $149/month, configured and probed correctly on day one. Staying self-hosted is the right call for plenty of teams: CORS errors and 403 Forbidden cover the two failures most often mistaken for this one, and custom domains covers the hostname side of putting Keycloak behind a name your users type.

entry.title: Data residency vs data sovereignty for your identity provider
entry.summary: Data residency is where your identity data is stored. Data sovereignty is whose law and whose hands reach it. What each fixes, tested on Keycloak 26.8.1.
entry.content:
Data residency is a statement about geography: your identity data is stored and processed in a named region and does not leave it. Data sovereignty is a statement about law and control: which legal systems can compel access to that data, and who holds the keys and the administrative credentials that make access technically possible. They are not the same claim, and the gap between them matters more for an identity provider than for almost any other system you run, because the IdP holds a record of every person who can sign in to anything you operate and a log of when and from where they did it. Below: both definitions, each applied to the four classes of data a Keycloak realm actually stores, the point where a region setting stops helping — demonstrated against Keycloak 26.8.1 — and the rubric European buyers have started scoring vendors with.

The difference in one table​

Data residencyData sovereignty
The question it answersWhere are the bytes written?Who can lawfully compel access, and who can technically perform it?
Determined byThe region you pick when the service is provisionedCorporate ownership, governing law, key custody, who holds admin access
Evidence a buyer can checkRegion configuration, data centre locations, subprocessor listCorporate structure, the processing agreement, a transfer impact assessment, key custody, access logs
How a vendor changes itA different regionA different owner, a different jurisdiction, or a different operating model
Who reviews it internallyInfrastructure and architectureLegal and the DPO
What it costs to verifyAn afternoonA contract negotiation

A third term turns up in the same conversations. Data localisation is a legal requirement that certain data stay in a country — it is residency imposed by a regulator rather than chosen by a buyer. Residency is the control; localisation is one of the reasons you might need it; sovereignty is a separate axis that residency alone does not move.

The practical consequence is that residency is cheap and verifiable, sovereignty is expensive and contestable, and most vendor marketing quietly substitutes the first for the second. When a page says "your data never leaves the EU" and the question you asked was "can a non-EU authority compel it", you have been answered on the wrong axis.

Why the gap is wider for an identity provider​

Most systems hold one kind of data. An identity provider holds four, and they do not behave the same way under either control. Everything below was run against a stock Keycloak 26.8.1:

docker run -d --name kc -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.1 start-dev

After creating a realm, a user and a confidential client, and performing one login:

$ kcadm.sh get events -r eu-demo --fields type,clientId,userId,ipAddress,time
[ { "time" : 1792402757656, "type" : "LOGIN", "clientId" : "portal",
    "userId" : "cb45f9ae-...", "ipAddress" : "172.17.0.1" } ]

$ kcadm.sh get clients/dbf8b3a4-.../user-sessions -r eu-demo
[ { "id" : "gCeFoM8Gbw5CEH-WxILJEf26", "username" : "anja",
    "ipAddress" : "172.17.0.1", "start" : 1792402757000 } ]
ClassWhat it isWhat residency settlesWhat residency leaves open
CredentialsPassword hashes — argon2id by default in 26.xWhere the hash sitsNothing, directly: a hash is not reversible. See the signing-key row, which makes that moot
ProfileUsername, email, name, attributes, group and role membershipWhere the records sitThey are readable in cleartext by anyone operating the database
SessionsActive sessions, each carrying a username and an IP addressWhere the session store sitsA session record is personal data about where your user was, not only that they signed in
EventsLogin and admin events, with IP, user id and client idWhere the event store sitsRetention. Turn events on and no eventsExpiration field appears at all, so events accumulate until you set one
Realm signing keysThe private keys that sign every token the realm issuesWhere the key material sitsWho can read it — the subject of the next section

Two of those deserve a sentence each. The IP address on a session and on an event makes login telemetry location data about your users, which is why "only metadata" is a weak defence for an IdP. And the retention default is genuinely absent rather than generous — this is the config immediately after switching event logging on:

$ kcadm.sh get events/config -r eu-demo
{ "eventsEnabled" : true, "eventsListeners" : [ "jboss-logging" ],
  "enabledEventTypes" : [ "LOGOUT", "LOGIN_ERROR", "LOGIN", "REFRESH_TOKEN" ],
  "adminEventsEnabled" : true, "adminEventsDetailsEnabled" : true }

No eventsExpiration key is returned until you set one. Setting it is one call — kcadm.sh update events/config -r eu-demo -s eventsExpiration=2592000 for thirty days — and on a realm that has been running for a year without it, doing so is not a free operation. The mechanics of purging a large event table are in user events in Keycloak and how we scaled Keycloak event storage.

The test a region setting cannot pass​

Here is the sharpest version of the distinction, and it is checkable on your own laptop in five minutes.

Generate a signing key yourself — the thing a buyer does when they want control rather than location — and load it into the realm with Keycloak's rsa key provider, which takes an existing PEM private key and certificate rather than generating one:

openssl genrsa -out eu-sign.key 2048
openssl req -new -x509 -key eu-sign.key -out eu-sign.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=eu-demo"

PK=$(grep -v '^-----' eu-sign.key | tr -d '\n')
CRT=$(grep -v '^-----' eu-sign.crt | tr -d '\n')

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin/realms/eu-demo/components \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"eu-imported-rsa","providerId":"rsa",
       "providerType":"org.keycloak.keys.KeyProvider",
       "config":{"priority":["200"],"active":["true"],"enabled":["true"],
                 "algorithm":["RS256"],
                 "privateKey":["'"$PK"'"],"certificate":["'"$CRT"'"]}}'

With priority 200 it becomes the active RS256 key, and the public half is immediately published to every relying party:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/realms/eu-demo/protocol/openid-connect/certs \
    | jq -r '.keys[] | "\(.kid)  \(.alg)  \(.use)"'
Kow7HwRH1GIYwD_q3nzWJHMHDD-6NlvXeSzaVcn_NoE  RS256  sig
rQLZRIk2xyyn2ZOp9Kp9oMpInO6Axnx0kgsZxSeP8SM  RSA-OAEP  enc
7oWmsgS6YGt3dM1zmGpZA8S1v_AwvrV2IcHFdWGF4f0  RS256  sig

Now read it back through the administrative API, the way a customer would:

$ curl -s ".../admin/realms/eu-demo/components/66cd252d-..." -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{
  "name": "eu-imported-rsa",
  "providerId": "rsa",
  "config": {
    "privateKey": [ "**********" ],
    "certificate": [ "MIIDBTCCAe2gAwIBAgIUP8OY..." ],
    "active": [ "true" ],
    "priority": [ "200" ],
    "algorithm": [ "RS256" ]
  }
}

Masked. The same is true of POST /admin/realms/eu-demo/partial-export, which returns 121 top-level keys of realm configuration with every private key either masked or omitted. That is the customer-facing path, and it behaves correctly.

Now take the operator's path — stop the server and run kc.sh export against the same database:

docker stop kc && docker cp kc:/opt/keycloak/data/. ./kcdata/
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/kcdata:/opt/keycloak/data" quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.1 \
  export --dir /opt/keycloak/data/export --realm eu-demo
$ grep -o '"privateKey"' kcdata/export/eu-demo-realm.json | wc -l
3
$ grep -o '\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*' kcdata/export/eu-demo-realm.json | wc -l
0

Three private keys, nothing masked, in an 83 KB file — the two keys Keycloak generated for the realm, plus the one I imported and which the API had just refused to show me. The client secret comes out in cleartext in the same file. And the exported key is not an equivalent key, it is the key:

$ openssl pkey -in roundtrip.pem -pubout | openssl sha256
SHA2-256(stdin)= ae9f19087063dc4a7ec22e4d74d9e9e85ef25d89d6aadfd4db2d289ccdb6c960
$ openssl pkey -in eu-sign.key -pubout | openssl sha256
SHA2-256(stdin)= ae9f19087063dc4a7ec22e4d74d9e9e85ef25d89d6aadfd4db2d289ccdb6c960

This is the whole argument in one measurement. Whoever can run that export holds the key that signs every token in the realm, and can therefore mint a valid token for any user without touching a password hash — which is why the irreversibility of argon2 protects less than it looks like it does. Residency decides which country that file is written in. It decides nothing at all about who is allowed to run the command, and that second question is sovereignty.

None of this is a Keycloak defect. An identity provider has to be able to sign, so some component has to be able to read the key; key custody is a deployment decision, not a product one. It is a defect in a procurement process that checks the region field and stops.

The rubric European buyers are starting to use​

If you need a vocabulary for this that is not a vendor's, the European Commission published one. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework, first presented in October 2025 for a tender under the Cloud III Dynamic Purchasing System, scores a provider on eight sovereignty objectives — strategic, legal and jurisdictional, data and AI, operational, supply chain, technology, security and compliance, and environmental — and assigns a Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Level, SEAL-0 to SEAL-4. The implementation guidance published on 1 June 2026 defines them:

LevelCommission's definition
SEAL-0No sovereignty. "Service, technology or operations under exclusive control of non-EU third parties, governed entirely by non-EU jurisdictions."
SEAL-1Jurisdictional sovereignty. "EU law formally applies with limited practical enforceability; service, technology or operations under exclusive control of non-EU third parties."
SEAL-2Data sovereignty. "EU jurisdictions apply, with material dependencies remain; service, technology or operations under indirect control of non-EU third parties."
SEAL-3Technological sovereignty. "EU jurisdictions apply, EU actors exercising meaningful but not full influence; service, technology or operations under marginal control of non-EU third parties."
SEAL-4Full digital sovereignty. "Technology and operations under complete EU control, subject only to EU jurisdiction, with no critical non-EU dependencies."

Three things in that document matter more than the labels.

First, the scoring rule: "the overall SEAL level is the lowest SEAL level achieved in any of the objectives." Sovereignty is scored as a floor, not an average. A vendor can be excellent on data location and still sit at the level its ownership earns, because strategic and jurisdictional sovereignty are their own objectives and no region setting touches them.

Second, what the data objective actually asks for. SOV-3 is not "stored in the EU"; its criteria include "ensuring that only the customer, not the provider, has effective control over cryptographic access to their data" and "strict confinement of storage and processing to European jurisdictions, with no fallback to third countries". That first clause is the export test above, written as a procurement question.

Third, the Commission's own caveat, from its lessons-learnt section: SEAL-4 "is not today relevant in the context of EU Sovereignty considering existing dependence to specific supply chains (chips, hardware)". In the April 2026 award the minimum was SEAL-2; the providers that did best reached SEAL-3. The top of the scale was not reached by anyone, which is a useful corrective to any vendor — European or not — claiming the whole of it.

The law that residency does not move​

The reason none of this collapses into "just pick Frankfurt" is a single sentence of US law. 18 U.S.C. § 2713, added by the CLOUD Act in March 2018, reads in full:

A provider of electronic communication service or remote computing service shall comply with the obligations of this chapter to preserve, backup, or disclose the contents of a wire or electronic communication and any record or other information pertaining to a customer or subscriber within such provider's possession, custody, or control, regardless of whether such communication, record, or other information is located within or outside of the United States.

Read the two operative phrases together. The test is possession, custody, or control; the location of the data is explicitly made irrelevant. A region choice is an answer to a question the statute declines to ask. What does move the analysis is the practical ability to obtain the data: who holds the keys, who can reach the control plane, which entity is the contracting processor, and what organisational separation actually exists between it and any non-EU parent. Those are sovereignty controls, and they are the ones worth negotiating.

Two facts we re-verified on 19 October 2026, because both move and both get misstated. The EU–US Data Privacy Framework is in force and listed as a current adequacy decision; Philippe Latombe's appeal against the General Court's dismissal of his challenge is pending before the Court of Justice as Case C-703/25 P, with no hearing announced. And FISA Section 702's statutory authority lapsed in June 2026 when Congress did not reauthorise it, while collection continues under Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court certifications approved in March 2026 and running to March 2027. A lapsed statute is not a dead programme, and anyone telling you otherwise is selling on a technicality.

What to ask an identity provider​

Ten minutes of questions that separate the two axes. A vendor who answers all ten in writing is being straight with you, whatever the answers are.

  1. Which region holds the realm database, the session store, the event store and the backups — and is the region fixed at creation?
  2. Which of your own systems (dashboard, ticketing, billing, monitoring, logging) sit outside that region?
  3. Who are the subprocessors, and do you commit to notice and an objection right before adding one?
  4. Can staff outside the EU administer an EU cluster? Under what controls, and are the access logs available to me?
  5. Where is the realm signing key held, who can read it, and can I supply or rotate it?
  6. Which legal entity is my counterparty, where is it incorporated, and who owns it?
  7. Which transfer mechanism covers each non-EU touchpoint, and will you share the transfer impact assessment?
  8. What is your contractual breach notification window, in hours?
  9. How many government or law-enforcement requests have you received, and what is your challenge-and-notify policy?
  10. What does an export contain, in what format, and what is the deletion commitment at the end of service?

Questions 1 to 3 are residency. Questions 4 to 7 are sovereignty. Questions 8 to 10 are what you actually live with. A vendor that answers 1 to 3 enthusiastically and goes quiet on 4 to 7 has told you something.

Where we stand​

We offer residency, and we do not offer sovereignty by ownership. Identity data for an EU cluster is stored and processed in Frankfurt (eu-central-1) with the standing backup in Ireland (eu-west-1), and is not replicated outside the EU. Your counterparty is Phase Two UK, Ltd, registered in England and Wales, company number 16815578, and the European Commission renewed its adequacy decision for the United Kingdom on 19 December 2025. Our parent, Phase Two, Inc., is incorporated in the United States, which is why § 2713 is quoted above rather than explained away, and our control plane runs in the US with a globally distributed engineering team — so administrative access to an EU cluster can come from outside the EU, which is a restricted transfer we disclose rather than discover with you.

On the key question specifically: realm signing keys for EU clusters are held in our key management service in the Frankfurt region. They are our keys in our KMS. We do not offer bring-your-own-key on hosted clusters today, and we would rather write that sentence than let a residency claim imply it. We are not certified under the Data Privacy Framework and do not rely on it. On question 9, what we do with a legal demand and how many we have received is on our government requests page; the count is still zero. The full data map, class by class, is in where your Keycloak data lives; the region list is in the regions documentation; what a token actually asserts, and what signs it, is in JWKS explained and the JWT tutorials.

If residency plus a written account of the sovereignty gap is enough for your risk assessment, our EU data residency page has the whole map, the subprocessor list and the questions our DPO is asked most. The Article 28 terms behind it are on the data processing agreement page.

Keycloak behaviour in this post was tested on 26.8.1 against the 26.8.1 server administration documentation. Regulatory facts were verified on 19 October 2026: the text of 18 U.S.C. § 2713 against the US Code as published by the Government Publishing Office; the Cloud Sovereignty Framework SEAL definitions against the Commission's implementation guidance of 1 June 2026; the UK and EU–US adequacy decisions against the Commission's adequacy decisions page; and the status of FISA Section 702 against reporting from June 2026 onward, with nothing enacted since.

entry.title: Migrating from Okta to Keycloak
entry.summary: How to migrate from Okta to Keycloak, tested on 26.8.1 — the app inventory that sets the schedule, why Okta never exports a password hash, and how to run both at once.
entry.content:
Migrating from Okta to Keycloak is not a user migration. The users are the easy part: Okta's Users API hands you profiles and group membership, and Keycloak's partial-import endpoint takes them. Two other things decide how long this takes. Okta will not give you password hashes — they are an import-only field, so every user either resets a password or authenticates through Okta one last time while you drain. And every SAML and OIDC application has to be re-pointed by hand, one at a time, because the assertion consumer URL, the entity ID and the signing certificate all change when the identity provider does.

So the schedule is set by the app inventory, not by the user count. A thousand users is one afternoon. Forty SAML apps is a quarter. Everything below was run against Keycloak 26.8.1 in start-dev, and the Okta side is from Okta's published API specification, read on 2026-10-19.

The short version​

  1. Inventory the apps first: GET /api/v1/apps, filter on signOnMode client-side, and count the SAML ones. That number is your project plan.
  2. Export users (GET /api/v1/users) and groups, and remember that the default listing omits deprovisioned users.
  3. In the target realm, in this order: set the unmanaged attribute policy, create the groups, create any identity providers your federated users came from.
  4. Convert the export and POST /admin/realms/{realm}/partialImport in batches of about 100.
  5. Verify the import by reading users back — three things vanish at HTTP 200 if step 3 was skipped.
  6. Decide the password story: reset everyone, or broker Okta and drain. There is no third option that moves hashes.
  7. Add Okta as an identity provider in Keycloak, with a first-broker-login flow that links to the accounts you just imported instead of duplicating them.
  8. Move apps one at a time to Keycloak, keeping Okta live behind it.
  9. When the last app is moved and the last user has logged in, remove the Okta identity provider and turn the tenant off.

What Okta gives you, and what it never will​

Okta objectLeaves the tenant?Lands in Keycloak as
User profile (profile.*)Yesuser fields + attributes
Okta user idYesan attribute — keep it, you need it for reconciliation
Group membershipYesgroup membership (groups must exist first)
Group rulesReadable (/api/v1/groups/rules)nothing — no equivalent, re-implement or flatten
App assignmentsYes, per appclient scope / role design you write yourself
SAML app settingsYes, per appa new SAML client, with new URLs and a new certificate
Password hashesNo—
MFA enrolmentsFactor list only, never the seed— users re-enrol
Okta sign-on policies, network zones, device assuranceReadableauthentication flows and conditions you design
Inline hooks, WorkflowsReadableauthenticator SPI, event listeners, or nothing
System logYes, 90 daysnot an import target

The password row is the one that decides your project. Okta's API reference describes the hash object as something that "may be specified in a password object when creating or updating a user, but not for other operations" — it is write-only, an on-ramp for people moving to Okta. Read a user back and credentials.password is an empty object. There is no support process that unseals it, which is a real difference from some other vendors, and worth knowing before you promise anyone a silent migration.

Inventory the apps before anything else​

Two gotchas here, both of which cost an afternoon if you meet them at the wrong moment.

GET /api/v1/apps cannot filter on signOnMode. Okta's specification lists the supported filter properties as id, status, credentials.signing.kid, settings.slo.enabled and name — that is the whole list. The signOnModes filter you may find in examples belongs to the app catalog endpoint, not to your installed apps. So pull everything and filter locally:

# 200 is the maximum page size; follow the `next` link, do not build your own cursor
curl -s -H "Authorization: SSWS $OKTA_TOKEN" \
  "https://$ORG/api/v1/apps?limit=200&filter=status+eq+%22ACTIVE%22" \
| jq -r '.[] | [.id, .signOnMode, .label] | @tsv' \
| sort -k2

Group the output by signOnMode. SAML_2_0 and OPENID_CONNECT are migrations you will schedule individually. SECURE_PASSWORD_STORE, BOOKMARK and BROWSER_PLUGIN are the password-vaulting and tile-only integrations — Keycloak does not do those at all, and pretending otherwise at the start of a project is how you end up explaining it at the end.

Then, per app, two calls that tell you who breaks when you move it:

curl -s -H "Authorization: SSWS $OKTA_TOKEN" "https://$ORG/api/v1/apps/$APP/users?limit=200"
curl -s -H "Authorization: SSWS $OKTA_TOKEN" "https://$ORG/api/v1/apps/$APP/groups?limit=200"

The SAML metadata endpoint is GET /api/v1/apps/{appId}/sso/saml/metadata, and it requires a kid query parameter naming the signing key. It returns Okta's metadata, which is useful as a record of what the service provider is currently trusting — the certificate in it is the one you are about to invalidate. Keep a copy per app; it is the fastest way to answer "what changed" when an app breaks a week later.

Export users and groups​

# default page size is 200; DEPROVISIONED users are omitted from a plain listing
curl -s -H "Authorization: SSWS $OKTA_TOKEN" \
  "https://$ORG/api/v1/users?limit=200" -D headers.txt \
| jq -c '.[]' >> users.ndjson
# then follow the rel="next" link from headers.txt until there isn't one

Okta's own documentation is explicit that a plain listing "omits users that have a status of DEPROVISIONED". If you want them — and for an audit trail you often do — ask for them with a search instead: ?search=status+eq+%22DEPROVISIONED%22. The distinction matters because a deprovisioned Okta user and a missing Okta user look identical in an export, and "why is this person gone" is a question that arrives three months after the cutover.

Group membership comes from the group side: GET /api/v1/groups then GET /api/v1/groups/{groupId}/users for each. Flatten that into a {oktaUserId: [groupName, ...]} map before you convert anything.

While you are there, read GET /api/v1/groups/rules. Okta group rules — "everyone in department X joins group Y" — have no Keycloak equivalent. They are either a thing your HR system does over SCIM after the move, or a thing you stop doing. Finding that out now is better than finding it out when the first new hire has no access.

Convert the export​

The status mapping is the only interesting part. Okta has eight user states and Keycloak has enabled plus required actions:

Okta statusKeycloak enabledRequired actionWhy
ACTIVEtrue—
PROVISIONEDtrueUPDATE_PASSWORDactivated, never set a password
STAGEDtrueUPDATE_PASSWORDnever activated
RECOVERYtrueUPDATE_PASSWORDmid-reset when you exported
PASSWORD_EXPIREDtrueUPDATE_PASSWORD
LOCKED_OUTtrue—lockout is brute-force state, not a user property; it does not transfer
SUSPENDEDfalse—
DEPROVISIONEDfalse—only present if you asked for them
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""okta_to_keycloak.py — convert an Okta user export into Keycloak partial-import batches.

    python3 okta_to_keycloak.py users.ndjson --memberships memberships.json \
        --out out/ --batch 100 --idp-alias google
"""
import argparse, json, os

STATUS = {
    "ACTIVE":           (True,  []),
    "PROVISIONED":      (True,  ["UPDATE_PASSWORD"]),
    "STAGED":           (True,  ["UPDATE_PASSWORD"]),
    "RECOVERY":         (True,  ["UPDATE_PASSWORD"]),
    "PASSWORD_EXPIRED": (True,  ["UPDATE_PASSWORD"]),
    "LOCKED_OUT":       (True,  []),
    "SUSPENDED":        (False, []),
    "DEPROVISIONED":    (False, []),
}
CORE = {"login", "email", "firstName", "lastName"}


def convert(okta, memberships, idp_alias):
    p = okta.get("profile", {})
    enabled, actions = STATUS.get(okta.get("status", "ACTIVE"), (True, []))

    attrs = {"oktaId": [okta["id"]]}
    for k, v in p.items():
        if k in CORE or v in (None, "", [], {}):
            continue
        attrs[k] = [str(x) for x in v] if isinstance(v, list) else [v]

    user = {
        "username": p["login"].lower(),
        "email": (p.get("email") or p["login"]).lower(),
        "firstName": p.get("firstName"),
        "lastName": p.get("lastName"),
        "enabled": enabled,
        "emailVerified": okta.get("status") in
            ("ACTIVE", "PASSWORD_EXPIRED", "LOCKED_OUT", "RECOVERY"),
        "attributes": attrs,
        "groups": ["/" + g for g in memberships.get(okta["id"], [])],
    }
    if actions:
        user["requiredActions"] = actions

    provider = (okta.get("credentials") or {}).get("provider") or {}
    if provider.get("type") == "FEDERATION" and idp_alias:
        # a user who signed in to Okta through Google or an upstream SAML IdP:
        # link them to the same provider in Keycloak, and never ask them for a password
        user["federatedIdentities"] = [{
            "identityProvider": idp_alias,
            "userId": okta["id"],
            "userName": p["login"].lower(),
        }]
        user.pop("requiredActions", None)
    return user


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("users")
    ap.add_argument("--memberships", help='JSON: {oktaUserId: ["group", ...]}')
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="out")
    ap.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=100)
    ap.add_argument("--idp-alias", default="")
    ap.add_argument("--if-exists", default="SKIP", choices=["FAIL", "SKIP", "OVERWRITE"])
    args = ap.parse_args()

    memberships = json.load(open(args.memberships)) if args.memberships else {}
    os.makedirs(args.out, exist_ok=True)

    users, groups = [], set()
    for line in open(args.users):
        if line.strip():
            u = convert(json.loads(line), memberships, args.idp_alias)
            groups.update(g.lstrip("/") for g in u["groups"])
            users.append(u)

    open(os.path.join(args.out, "groups.txt"), "w").write("\n".join(sorted(groups)) + "\n")
    for n, i in enumerate(range(0, len(users), args.batch), start=1):
        json.dump({"ifResourceExists": args.if_exists, "users": users[i:i + args.batch]},
                  open(os.path.join(args.out, f"batch-{n:03d}.json"), "w"), indent=1)
    print(f"{len(users)} users, {len(groups)} groups -> {args.out}/")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It writes groups.txt as well as the batches, because of the next section.

Import it, then check what did not arrive​

Partial import is a single transaction per request, which is the good news: a batch either lands completely or not at all. The bad news is the failure modes are inconsistent. Three things in an Okta-shaped payload behave differently from each other, and only one of them tells you.

A group that does not exist fails the whole request, loudly but unhelpfully. The response is a bare 500:

{"error":"unknown_error","error_description":"For more on this error consult the server log."}

and the actual cause is only in the server log:

ERROR [org.keycloak.services.error.KeycloakErrorHandler] Uncaught server error:
java.lang.RuntimeException: Unable to find group specified by path: /Engineering

Nothing was written. Create the groups from groups.txt first:

while read -r g; do
  kcadm create groups -r acme -s "name=$g"
done < out/groups.txt

Realm roles are the opposite — a role named in realmRoles that does not exist is created for you, and the mapping is applied. Convenient, and worth knowing so you are not surprised by a realm full of roles you did not design.

Attributes disappear silently. A realm created today has no unmanaged attribute policy, so oktaId, department, employeeNumber and the rest are dropped — with "added": 5 and HTTP 200 in the response. Set the policy before importing:

kcadm get users/profile -r acme > up.json
jq '.unmanagedAttributePolicy = "ADMIN_EDIT"' up.json > up2.json
kcadm update users/profile -r acme -f up2.json

(Declaring each attribute explicitly in the user profile is the tidier choice for anything you intend to keep; the unmanaged policy is the fast one for a migration.)

Federated identities disappear silently too, if the identity provider alias is not already configured in the realm. Import a user whose federatedIdentities names google before the google provider exists and the response is "added": 1 — and the link is simply not there. Create the identity providers first, even as placeholders.

With all three in place, the import is unremarkable, which is the goal:

added 5 skipped 0

isaac.brock@example.com  enabled=True  actions=-                oktaId=00ub0oNGTSWTBKOLGLNR
    groups: ['/All Employees', '/Engineering']
    links: []
sam@partner.example      enabled=True  actions=-                oktaId=00u3fed4wQRSTUVWXYZA
    groups: ['/Partners']
    links: [('google', '00u3fed4wQRSTUVWXYZA')]
lee.ng@example.com       enabled=True  actions=UPDATE_PASSWORD  oktaId=00u2bcd8xYGHIJKLMNOP
    groups: ['/All Employees', '/Engineering']
    links: []
dana@example.com         enabled=False actions=-                oktaId=00u1ero7vZFVEIYLWPBN
    groups: ['/All Employees', '/Support']
    links: []

One more thing to know before you re-run anything: ifResourceExists: "OVERWRITE" does not update users in place. It deletes and recreates them, and the Keycloak user id changes. If an application has already stored sub as a foreign key, a re-run of the import breaks it. Use SKIP for repeat runs and reconcile deliberately against the oktaId attribute.

Passwords: pick one of two, because there is no third​

OptionWhat users experienceWhat it costs you
Reset everythingOne password-reset mail each, at cutoverSupport load in a single week; anyone who ignores the mail is locked out
Broker Okta and drainNothing, until you turn Okta offOkta stays live and paid for the length of the drain
Verify against Okta on first login (ROPC bridge)Nothing; the password follows themOnly works for password-only users; see below

The third row is the one people ask for, so here is exactly where it stops. Okta supports the OAuth 2.0 password grant, which means a bridge — a user storage provider that verifies a typed password against Okta once, then stores it in Keycloak — is technically possible. The keycloak-user-migration plugin implements that pattern against two REST endpoints you supply, a GET that returns the user and a POST that answers 200 if the password is right.

The limits are real and Okta documents them: the grant has to be enabled both on the app and on the authorization server, Okta describes the flow as not recommended and a last resort, and its own list of conditions for using it includes that you do not need your users to use multifactor authentication. So the bridge covers password-only users, and anyone on a factor still needs a reset. In most enterprise Okta tenants that is the wrong way round — which is why, for the enterprise case, brokering is the better answer and this section is mostly here to stop you spending a week on the other one.

One interaction to plan for: a user created by partial import is a local Keycloak user with no federation link, so a storage provider is never consulted for them. The bridge only fires for users Keycloak does not already have. Pre-import profiles or let the bridge create users on first login — doing both to the same person just means the bridge never runs.

Run both at once: broker Okta, then drain​

This is the migration that works for an organisation with apps it cannot move in one night. Keycloak becomes the front door immediately; Okta becomes an upstream identity provider behind it; apps move one at a time; the last step is deleting the provider.

Add Okta as an OIDC identity provider in Keycloak, pointed at https://$ORG/.well-known/openid-configuration (or your custom authorization server's discovery document), with a Keycloak-redirect-URI app registered on the Okta side.

The part that needs configuring is what happens on the first brokered login for a user you already imported. The stock first broker login flow asks them to confirm:

Account already exists
User with email isaac.brock@example.com already exists. How do you want to continue?
  [Review profile]  [Add to existing account]

That is correct behaviour for a public IdP and wrong for this job: you control both ends, and every one of these users is a person you already imported. Replace the flow with one that links automatically:

kcadm create authentication/flows -r acme \
  -s alias=okta-auto-link -s providerId=basic-flow -s topLevel=true -s builtIn=false
kcadm create authentication/flows/okta-auto-link/executions/execution -r acme \
  -s provider=idp-create-user-if-unique
kcadm create authentication/flows/okta-auto-link/executions/execution -r acme \
  -s provider=idp-auto-link
# set both executions to ALTERNATIVE, then point the provider at the flow
kcadm update identity-provider/instances/okta -r acme \
  -s firstBrokerLoginFlowAlias=okta-auto-link

Tested on 26.8.1: with that flow, a brokered login for an imported user goes straight through to the application with no prompt, the realm user count does not change, and the link lands on the existing account:

[{"identityProvider":"okta","userId":"a739cff6-f94e-4707-972c-89b10ae56ff7",
  "userName":"isaac.brock@example.com"}]

Two warnings, both of which bite in practice.

idp-auto-link matches on the username in the brokered token. If Okta sends preferred_username: rita and you imported rita@example.com, nothing matches and the user sees Invalid username or password — a message that sends everyone looking at the password when the problem is the join key. The event tells the truth and is worth having a listener for:

type="IDENTITY_PROVIDER_FIRST_LOGIN_ERROR" error="invalid_user_credentials"
identity_provider="okta" identity_provider_identity="rita"

Import the username in the form Okta will send, which for most tenants is profile.login.

Automatic linking trusts the upstream provider completely. Anyone who can set an email or username at the IdP can take over the matching local account. During a cutover you own the IdP, so that is an acceptable trade for a week or a quarter. It is not a permanent setting: remove the flow when the drain is done, along with the provider.

What you lose, plainly​

  • MFA enrolments. The factors API lists what a user enrolled; the shared secret appears only in an enrolment response. Everyone re-enrols. Schedule it, communicate it, and expect it to be the single largest source of tickets. (If you issued hardware TOTP tokens and still hold the seed file, those can be re-provisioned — that is the one exception.)
  • Okta Verify push, device trust and FastPass. No equivalent. Keycloak has WebAuthn and OTP, which is a different security model, not a port.
  • Group rules, sign-on policies, network zones. Readable, not portable. They become authentication flows, conditions and client policies that you design.
  • Inline hooks and Workflows. Rewritten against the authenticator SPI or an event listener.
  • Outbound provisioning to downstream apps. This is the one people miss, so it has its own section below.
  • The Okta dashboard tile. Keycloak has no app portal. IdP-initiated SAML gets you part of the way — we wrote up how that flow actually works — and the rest is a page of links somebody maintains.
  • The system log, after 90 days. Export what you need for audit before the tenant closes.

SCIM: the arrow turns around​

If Okta provisions users into your SaaS applications, read this twice. Okta's documentation is clear about the direction: "Okta acts as the SCIM client, sending requests to your SCIM server to manage the user and group lifecycle." Okta pushes out to downstream apps.

Keycloak's SCIM support, promoted to supported in 26.8.0, is the other side of that arrow. Keycloak is the SCIM server: an HR system or an identity governance platform pushes users into a realm. Nothing in core Keycloak pushes users out to Workday, Slack or Zoom the way Okta's provisioning tab does. A realm-side toggle plus a service-account client gets you the inbound half — the mechanics are in our SCIM API tutorial — and the outbound half is a separate decision: keep Okta running for provisioning only, buy an IGA tool, or drive the downstream APIs from Keycloak events.

What does carry across cleanly is identity continuity. Map a user-profile attribute to the SCIM externalId and populate it with the Okta user id you kept in oktaId, and any system that was addressing people by Okta id keeps working after the tenant is gone. That one mapping is worth doing on day one, because it is nearly free then and a reconciliation project later.

A cutover order that works​

  1. Inventory apps, groups, group rules and policies. Decide what is not coming.
  2. Stand up the realm: unmanaged attribute policy, groups, identity providers, user profile attributes including the externalId mapping.
  3. Import users, with SKIP, in batches of 100. Verify by reading them back, not by reading the response.
  4. Broker Okta with the auto-link flow. Test with one real account before anyone else sees it.
  5. Move apps one at a time, lowest-traffic first, each with its own rollback: the old Okta app stays configured until the new one is proven.
  6. Watch the drain. Users who have never logged in through Keycloak still only exist as imported profiles; the brokered login count is your progress bar.
  7. Cut the tether: remove the identity provider, delete the auto-link flow, require password or passkey enrolment, export the Okta system log, close the tenant.

Step 5 is where the quarter goes. Everything above it is a week.

If you are weighing the move rather than running it, the Keycloak and Okta comparison covers what you give up in product terms, and the production readiness checklist is the other half of "Keycloak is free" — the half that is not.

Running Keycloak yourself is a real job on top of the migration, and the two are easier apart: managed Keycloak means the cutover is the only project you are running that quarter. If you want someone who has done this before to plan the app order and sit on the drain with you, talk to us about migrating to Keycloak.

entry.title: "Restart login cookie not found" in Keycloak
entry.summary: Keycloak's "Restart login cookie not found" means no KC_RESTART cookie arrived, never that it expired. Four branches, five causes, one fix. Tested on 26.8.0.
entry.content:
"Restart login cookie not found. It may have expired; it may have been deleted or cookies are disabled in your browser." Keycloak shows this on a dead-end HTTP 400 page, and the message is more confident than it should be. It means exactly one thing: the request arrived with no KC_RESTART cookie at all. Not a stale one, not a rejected one. None. That cookie has no expiry to run out, so "it may have expired" is the one explanation that is never true. A rejected cookie produces a different message. And the page tells the user to "Click Back to Application", which on a default client renders no link to click.

Here is what the cookie is for, how to tell in one log line which failure you have, and the one client field that turns the dead end into a recoverable page.

Everything below was reproduced against quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.0 in start-dev.

What KC_RESTART is​

Keycloak sets three cookies when you hit the authorization endpoint:

Set-Cookie: AUTH_SESSION_ID=<snip>;Path=/realms/demo/;Secure;HttpOnly;SameSite=None
Set-Cookie: KC_AUTH_SESSION_HASH="<snip>";Path=/realms/demo/;Max-Age=60;Secure;SameSite=None
Set-Cookie: KC_RESTART=<snip>;Path=/realms/demo/;Secure;HttpOnly;SameSite=None

AUTH_SESSION_ID points at the server-side authentication session, which lives for the realm's Login timeout (accessCodeLifespanLogin, 1800 seconds out of the box), described in the admin console as "Max time a user has to complete a login."

KC_RESTART is the fallback. It is an encrypted JWE (alg=dir, enc=A256GCM) sealed with the realm's AES key, carrying the client id, the redirect URI, the protocol and the client notes: enough to rebuild the flow from scratch. It measured 836 bytes on a realm with one plain OIDC client, it has no Max-Age, and Keycloak deletes it the moment a login completes. No Max-Age means it is a browser-session cookie: it dies when the browser session does, and never a minute sooner.

So the auth session is what times out, and the restart cookie is what rescues you when it does.

The four branches, and how to tell them apart​

When a request reaches /realms/<realm>/login-actions/* and the authentication session is not there, these are the four outcomes. The authorization endpoint itself never produces any of them, because it always starts a fresh flow. If you are seeing this error, the URL in the address bar contains login-actions.

What Keycloak hasHTTPWhat the user seesEvents logged
A usable KC_RESTART302The login page again, with "Your login attempt timed out. Login will start from the beginning."expired_code with restart_after_timeout="true"
No KC_RESTART, no SSO session400"Restart login cookie not found…"cookie_not_found
A KC_RESTART it cannot use400"An error occurred, please login again through your application."invalid_code, then cookie_not_found
No KC_RESTART, but a live SSO session302 to the clienterror=temporarily_unavailable&error_description=authentication_expiredalready_logged_in

The last row is checked after the other two failures, so an existing SSO session replaces the error page rather than adding to it. That is the case the user never sees.

Two things fall out of the table. First, a plain login timeout does not produce this error. With the restart cookie still in the browser you get a silent restart and a polite banner. If you are seeing the error, the cookie is gone, which means the browser never had it or threw it away.

Second, error="cookie_not_found" in the event log is not diagnostic on its own: rows two and three both log it. The distinguishing mark is whether an invalid_code event precedes it in the same request:

# Realm Settings → Sessions → Events, or:
kcadm.sh update events/config -r demo -s eventsEnabled=true \
  -s 'enabledEventTypes=["LOGIN","LOGIN_ERROR"]'
kcadm.sh get events -r demo -q type=LOGIN_ERROR -q max=10
[ { "type": "LOGIN_ERROR", "clientId": "webapp",
    "ipAddress": "172.17.0.1", "error": "cookie_not_found" } ]

One cookie_not_found by itself is this error. An invalid_code immediately before it means the cookie did arrive and Keycloak refused it. That happens when the realm's AES key has been regenerated since the cookie was issued, when the client in the cookie has been deleted, or when the cookie belongs to a different client than the client_id in the URL. Deleting and recreating a realm's aes-generated key provider invalidates every outstanding KC_RESTART in every user's browser at once; so does restoring a realm from an export.

The five ways the cookie goes missing​

1. The login page was opened in one cookie jar and submitted from another. A login URL that gets bookmarked, forwarded, pasted into a chat, or opened by a password manager in a fresh window carries a valid session_code and no cookies. Both the GET and the POST of that URL return the error. This is the most common cause and the least interesting one: the link was never reusable.

2. The browser threw the cookies away in between. KC_RESTART and AUTH_SESSION_ID are both session cookies. A browser restart, "clear cookies on quit", closing the private window, or a mobile OS evicting a backgrounded tab all discard them while the login page is still on screen. The user comes back, clicks Sign In, and lands here.

3. The cookies never reached the browser at all. Keycloak marks all three Secure; SameSite=None unconditionally, so plain HTTP on a real hostname, an unset proxy-headers, a hostname the form posts to that the user never visited, or a proxy stripping a path prefix will all silently drop them. That family is the subject of its own post. The Keycloak infinite redirect loop at login covers the diagnostics and the four fixes, and it is worth ruling out first if the error is reproducible rather than occasional.

4. The login page is in an iframe. SameSite=None is necessary for a third-party context but not sufficient: Safari blocks third-party cookies by default and will refuse them outright, and the flow dies at the first POST. Keycloak's own position is that the browser wins — its JavaScript adapter disables the session status iframe when it detects this. Use a top-level redirect for the login itself.

5. It is not a user. Uptime monitors, synthetic checks, load tests and crawlers replay captured login URLs without a cookie jar, and each attempt logs cookie_not_found. Every reproduction in this post was produced with curl and no cookie jar, which is precisely what your monitoring does. Before chasing a user-facing bug, check whether the events cluster on one IP or one user agent.

Make the page recoverable: set the client's Home URL​

The message ends with "Click Back to Application to login again." Whether that link exists depends on a client field most people leave blank. Keycloak's error.ftl renders it only when the client has a base URL:

<#if client?? && client.baseUrl?has_content>
    <p><a id="backToApplication" href="${client.baseUrl}">${msg("backToApplication")}</a></p>
</#if>

A client created through the admin console or kcadm has no baseUrl by default, so the error page comes back with zero links on it: a genuine dead end, telling the user to click something that is not there. Set it and the link appears:

kcadm.sh update clients/<id> -r demo -s baseUrl=https://app.example.com/
<a id="backToApplication" href="https://app.example.com/">« Back to Application</a>

That is Clients → your client → Settings → Home URL in the admin console. It costs nothing, it applies to every Keycloak error page, and it converts the most common unrecoverable state in the login flow into one click.

"Cookie not found" is the same error​

If you are searching for "Cookie not found. Please make sure cookies are enabled in your browser.", you are looking at this error on an older server. Both strings are the same message key, cookieNotFoundMessage, raised from the same code path. The wording changed in the 26.1 line: 26.0 and earlier shipped the short sentence, 26.1 and later ship the long one. Nothing about the behaviour changed with it.

Stop it recurring​

There is no lifespan to tune here and no KC_RESTART setting to add. The cookie either arrives or it does not. What you can do:

  1. Set Home URL on every client. One field, and the dead-end page gains an exit.
  2. Handle authentication_expired in the application. When the SSO session is alive but the tab's auth session is not, Keycloak redirects to the client with error=temporarily_unavailable&error_description=authentication_expired rather than showing a page. Keycloak's guidance is to immediately resubmit the authentication request, which succeeds silently against the existing SSO session. An app that treats it as a hard failure shows the user an error for a state Keycloak already recovered from.
  3. Fix the cookie transport before anything else if the error is reproducible rather than intermittent. Reproducible means configuration; intermittent means browsers and bots.
  4. Separate the bots from the users in the event log before estimating impact, and raise the realm's Login timeout only if real users are genuinely taking more than 30 minutes to sign in — session and token timeouts covers what else that setting moves.

This error is cheap to diagnose once you know that it describes an absent cookie rather than an expired one, and that the event log distinguishes the two cases it covers. The expensive part is usually everything underneath it — the proxy, the hostnames, the TLS chain that decides whether the cookies arrive. If you would rather not own that, Phase Two runs managed Keycloak with a 30-day Starter trial from $149/month, configured correctly on day one. Staying self-hosted is the right call for plenty of teams: the redirect loop post covers the transport failures that cause most of these, invalid_grant covers what breaks after the login page succeeds, and the production checklist has the proxy and hostname settings in one place.

entry.title: Where your Keycloak data lives: Frankfurt, Ireland, and what leaves the EU
entry.summary: Where Phase Two stores each class of your Keycloak data, Frankfurt and Ireland, who can reach it, what runs in the US, and which company you contract with.
entry.content:
Here is where your Keycloak data lives with us. The Keycloak database, sessions, event store, backups and realm signing keys for an EU cluster run in AWS Frankfurt (eu-central-1), with backups in Ireland (eu-west-1), and are never replicated outside the EU. Three things of ours do run in the United States: the dashboard you sign in to, support tickets, and billing. You contract with Phase Two UK, Ltd, registered in England and Wales, company number 16815578. Our parent company, Phase Two, Inc., is incorporated in the United States, and our control plane runs there, so administrators outside the EU can reach your cluster in order to operate it. Under Chapter V of the GDPR that access is a restricted transfer, and we would rather write it down here than have you find it in a risk assessment.

What your identity provider actually holds​

Before you can say where data lives you have to enumerate it, and the honest way to do that is against a running server rather than from a diagram. Everything below was run against Keycloak 26.8.0:

docker run -d --name kc -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.0 start-dev

After creating a realm, one user and one client and performing a single login, four endpoints return four classes of personal data:

$ kcadm.sh get users -r eu-demo -q username=anja --fields username,email,firstName,lastName
[ { "username": "anja", "firstName": "Anja", "lastName": "Keller", "email": "anja@example.de" } ]

$ kcadm.sh get users/6734fb1b-.../credentials -r eu-demo
[ { "type": "password", "createdDate": 1791799823228,
    "credentialData": "{\"hashIterations\":5,\"algorithm\":\"argon2\",
      \"additionalParameters\":{\"memory\":[\"7168\"],\"type\":[\"id\"],\"parallelism\":[\"1\"]}}" } ]

$ kcadm.sh get clients/0c98853f-.../user-sessions -r eu-demo --fields username,ipAddress,start
[ { "username": "anja", "ipAddress": "172.17.0.1", "start": 1791799828000 } ]

$ kcadm.sh get events -r eu-demo --fields type,clientId,userId,ipAddress,time
[ { "time": 1791799828405, "type": "LOGIN", "clientId": "portal",
    "userId": "6734fb1b-...", "ipAddress": "172.17.0.1" } ]

Profile, credential, session, event. A fifth class, the realm signing keys, comes back from kcadm.sh get keys, and it matters because whoever holds them can mint a token for any user in the realm.

Two details are worth stopping on. The session and the event both carry an IP address, so a login record is personal data about where your user was, not only that they signed in. And the default event configuration has no eventsExpiration field at all, so saved events accumulate until you set one. That retention decision is the controller's, which means yours: see user events in Keycloak and the audit log documentation.

Where each class lives​

What Keycloak holdsStored inWho can reach itLeaves the EU?
Users, credentials, groups, roles, client configFrankfurt eu-central-1Phase Two operations staff, including staff outside the EUNo
Sessions and cacheFrankfurt eu-central-1Phase Two operations staff, including staff outside the EUNo
Event store, login and admin eventsFrankfurt eu-central-1Phase Two operations staff, including staff outside the EUNo
BackupsIreland eu-west-1Phase Two operations staff, including staff outside the EUNo
Realm signing keysFrankfurt, AWS KMSPhase Two operations staffNo
Cluster logs and metricsFrankfurt eu-central-1Phase Two engineering, including staff outside the EUNo
Dashboard account metadataUnited StatesPhase Two staffYes
Support tickets and attachmentsUnited StatesPhase Two support staffYes
Billing and invoicingUnited StatesPhase Two finance staffYes

A cluster's region is fixed at creation and cannot be changed afterwards, so check it against your residency requirement before you launch. Ireland is the standing backup on every EU cluster, on every plan, at no extra cost; running a primary cluster there is a separate, paid option, and the full list is in the regions documentation.

Stored in the EU is not the same as touched only in the EU​

The last three rows are our business systems rather than your end users' identity data, and they are in the table because a version printing only the first six would be the more flattering document and the less useful one. One of them has a practical consequence: ticketing runs in the United States, so send us realm names, client IDs, error strings and correlation IDs, and do not paste user records into a ticket.

The larger point is in the third column. Our control plane, meaning provisioning, monitoring, alerting and ticketing, is a single instance in the United States, and our engineering team is spread across several countries. Operating your cluster, upgrading it, restoring it, responding at three in the morning, means reaching into it, and some of the people doing that are outside the EU.

Remote access to EU-stored data from a third country is itself a restricted transfer under Chapter V of the GDPR. It is covered by the Standard Contractual Clauses in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, incorporated into our data processing agreement along with a transfer impact assessment we will share on request. Access is limited to named operations roles and logged internally. One limitation stated plainly: those logs are examined in our SOC 2 Type II audit but are not exposed to customers today, and we would like to change that.

Who you contract with, and what that does not buy you​

Phase Two UK, Ltd is the contracting party for customers in the EU and the UK. The European Commission renewed its adequacy decision for the United Kingdom on 19 December 2025, valid until 27 December 2031, so an EU-to-UK transfer needs no additional safeguard.

What the UK entity does not buy you is immunity. Phase Two, Inc. is incorporated in the United States, and under the US CLOUD Act a provider subject to US jurisdiction can be compelled to disclose data in its "possession, custody, or control" wherever that data is stored. We do not claim to sit outside that. What we can tell you is what we do with a request, published on our government requests page: route it to one place, challenge what is overbroad, redirect it to you where we can, notify you unless prohibited, disclose the minimum, and publish the count. To date that count is zero.

What we do not claim​

  • We do not describe ourselves as sovereign, and we will not hold SecNumCloud qualification: it requires European ownership a US-parented company cannot satisfy.
  • We do not offer bring-your-own-key on hosted clusters. Realm signing keys for EU clusters sit in Frankfurt and do not leave the EU, but they are our keys in our KMS.
  • We are not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and do not rely on it as a transfer mechanism.
  • Support is in English only.
  • Our contractual breach notification window is 48 to 72 hours. NIS2 gives you 24 hours for an early warning, so raise this during contracting rather than discovering the gap during an incident.

Checking it, and leaving​

An exit claim is worth as much as the export behind it. A realm configuration export is one API call, and returned 121 top-level keys for a stock realm in under a second:

curl -s -X POST \
  "$KC/admin/realms/eu-demo/partial-export?exportClients=true&exportGroupsAndRoles=true" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -o realm.json

Note what that does not contain: users. partial-export returns configuration, so user records come from the Admin API or from kc.sh export --users different_files, and credentials come from a database dump we provide on request. Deletion at the end of service is an Article 28(3)(g) commitment carried out on request; we do not yet issue a certificate of deletion, and if your risk assessment needs one, ask and we will put it in your contract. For the same guarantees inside your own realm, see the offboarding tutorial and how we scaled Keycloak event storage.
